comments.value: `<` before a literal is a comparison operator, not type arguments
a second `<` after the operand opens no nested list — nothing closes one, so the
line is a chained comparison
a parenthesized ternary operand is a comparison, not a `(b?: T) => ...` function type
a `>` inside an array literal belongs to the array, not the relational chain
an indexed member access after `<` is a comparison operand, not an indexed access
type; the `,` that follows it belongs to the enclosing argument, element, or
property list, whatever the index is
richer index contents are comparison operands too when no `>` closes the list
arithmetic inside the index is not a type, so the list stays a comparison even
when a `>` closes it; a negated operand and the logical and relational operators
are expressions too, never types
a shift operator after the indexed operand continues the comparison chain — the
`>` run belongs to the operator, not to a type-argument close
an identifier that merely starts with `extends` is a fresh statement on the next
line (ASI), not a type constraint
genuine instantiation with a literal/keyword/object/tuple/numeric type arg, or a
function type with an optional param, still parses as type arguments
a generic nested inside a tuple or object-type arg still parses as type arguments
a template literal after the closing `>` is a tagged template on the
instantiation, not a comparison
an indexed access, array, or conditional type argument still parses as type
arguments — the closing `>` is followed by a call
every index content that is itself a valid type — union, intersection, nested
index, numeric literal, and conditional — makes the list type arguments
a numeric literal index continues into a type exactly as a reference index does —
union, intersection, and conditional forms are type arguments whichever operand
kind opens them, and an exponent's own sign belongs to the literal
